stem:
Which of the statements about the reaction below are incorrect?

\(2\text{PbO}(s) + \text{C}(s) \rightarrow 2\text{Pb}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)\)

(a) Lead is getting reduced.

(b) Carbon dioxide is getting oxidised.

(c) Carbon is getting oxidised.

(d) Lead oxide is getting reduced.
solution:
Take the four statements one at a time.

- **(a) Lead is getting reduced — INCORRECT.** What loses oxygen here is lead *oxide*, not lead. Lead is the product of that reduction, not the thing being reduced.
- **(b) Carbon dioxide is getting oxidised — INCORRECT.** Carbon dioxide is a product. It is formed *by* the oxidation of carbon; nothing oxidises it in this reaction.
- (c) Carbon is getting oxidised — correct. Carbon gains oxygen to become \(\text{CO}_2\).
- (d) Lead oxide is getting reduced — correct. \(\text{PbO}\) loses oxygen to become \(\text{Pb}\).

The question asks which statements are **incorrect**, so the answer is (a) and (b).
groundedIn: §1.2.5 — oxidation is the gain of oxygen, reduction is the loss of oxygen; the worked redox example is Eq. (1.31), \(\text{ZnO} + \text{C} \rightarrow \text{Zn} + \text{CO}\).

stem:
\(\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{Al} \rightarrow \text{Al}_2\text{O}_3 + 2\text{Fe}\)

The above reaction is an example of a
solution:
Aluminium is more reactive than iron, so it displaces iron from iron(III) oxide. One element (aluminium) displaces another element (iron) from its compound, which is the definition of a **displacement reaction**.

It is not a combination reaction (there is more than one product), not a decomposition reaction (there is more than one reactant), and not a double displacement reaction — that would need two compounds exchanging ions, whereas here one reactant is a free element.
groundedIn: §1.2.3 — 'when an element displaces another element from its compound, a displacement reaction occurs'.

stem: What happens when dilute hydrochloric acid is added to iron filings? Tick the correct answer.

options.label: A
options.text: Hydrogen gas and iron chloride are produced.

options.label: B
options.text: Chlorine gas and iron hydroxide are produced.

options.label: D
options.text: Iron salt and water are produced.

solution:
Iron is more reactive than hydrogen, so it displaces hydrogen from dilute hydrochloric acid:

\(\text{Fe}(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{FeCl}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)\)

So hydrogen gas is evolved and iron(II) chloride is left in solution. Option (b) is wrong because chlorine is not released; option (c) is wrong because a reaction does occur; option (d) is wrong because water is formed when an acid reacts with a *base*, not with a metal.
groundedIn: Activity 1.2 — dilute sulphuric acid on zinc evolves hydrogen gas, the same metal-plus-acid pattern; and §1.2.3 on displacement.

stem: What is a balanced chemical equation? Why should chemical equations be balanced?
solution:
A **balanced chemical equation** is one in which the number of atoms of each element is the same on the reactant side and on the product side.

Equations must be balanced because of the **law of conservation of mass**: matter is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction. Atoms of one element do not change into atoms of another, none disappear from the mixture and none appear from elsewhere — a reaction only breaks and remakes bonds between the atoms already present. An unbalanced equation would therefore describe a reaction in which mass changes, which is impossible.
groundedIn: §1.1.2 for the definition, and §1.2 — 'atoms of one element do not change into those of another element. Nor do atoms disappear from the mixture or appear from elsewhere.'

context: Translate the following statements into chemical equations and then balance them.
stem: Hydrogen gas combines with nitrogen to form ammonia.
solution:
\(3\text{H}_2(g) + \text{N}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{NH}_3(g)\)

Check: H 6 and 6; N 2 and 2.
groundedIn: §1.1.2, the hit-and-trial balancing method.

context: Translate the following statements into chemical equations and then balance them.
stem: Hydrogen sulphide gas burns in air to give water and sulphur dioxide.
solution:
\(2\text{H}_2\text{S}(g) + 3\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) + 2\text{SO}_2(g)\)

'Burns in air' means the gas reacts with the oxygen of the air, so \(\text{O}_2\) is the second reactant.

Check: H 4 and 4; S 2 and 2; O 6 and 6 (2 in the water, 4 in the sulphur dioxide).
groundedIn: §1.1.2, the hit-and-trial balancing method.

context: Translate the following statements into chemical equations and then balance them.
stem: Barium chloride reacts with aluminium sulphate to give aluminium chloride and a precipitate of barium sulphate.
solution:
\(3\text{BaCl}_2(aq) + \text{Al}_2(\text{SO}_4)_3(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{AlCl}_3(aq) + 3\text{BaSO}_4(s)\)

Check: Ba 3 and 3; Cl 6 and 6; Al 2 and 2; S 3 and 3; O 12 and 12. Barium sulphate is the precipitate, so it takes \((s)\).
groundedIn: §1.1.2 for balancing, §1.2.4 for the double displacement pattern.

context: Translate the following statements into chemical equations and then balance them.
stem: Potassium metal reacts with water to give potassium hydroxide and hydrogen gas.
solution:
\(2\text{K}(s) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow 2\text{KOH}(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)\)

Check: K 2 and 2; O 2 and 2; H 4 and 4 — two hydrogen atoms in the two \(\text{OH}\) groups and two more in the \(\text{H}_2\) molecule.
groundedIn: §1.1.2 for balancing; §1.2.3 for a metal displacing hydrogen.

context: Balance the following chemical equations.
stem: \(\text{HNO}_3 + \text{Ca(OH)}_2 \rightarrow \text{Ca(NO}_3)_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)
solution:
\(2\text{HNO}_3 + \text{Ca(OH)}_2 \rightarrow \text{Ca(NO}_3)_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

The calcium nitrate on the right needs two nitrate groups, so put 2 before \(\text{HNO}_3\). That gives 2 hydrogen atoms from the acid and 2 more from the hydroxide, which is 4 in all, so 2 water molecules balance them.

Check: H 4 and 4; N 2 and 2; Ca 1 and 1; O 8 and 8.
groundedIn: §1.1.2, the hit-and-trial balancing method.

context: Balance the following chemical equations.
stem: \(\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + \text{H}_2\text{O}\)
solution:
\(2\text{NaOH} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}\)

Sodium sulphate carries two sodium atoms, so 2 is needed before \(\text{NaOH}\); the 4 hydrogen atoms then present balance as 2 water molecules.

Check: Na 2 and 2; O 6 and 6; H 4 and 4; S 1 and 1.
groundedIn: §1.1.2, the hit-and-trial balancing method.

context: Balance the following chemical equations.
stem: \(\text{NaCl} + \text{AgNO}_3 \rightarrow \text{AgCl} + \text{NaNO}_3\)
solution:
\(\text{NaCl} + \text{AgNO}_3 \rightarrow \text{AgCl} + \text{NaNO}_3\)

This equation is **already balanced** as printed: Na 1 and 1; Cl 1 and 1; Ag 1 and 1; N 1 and 1; O 3 and 3. No coefficients need to be added.
groundedIn: §1.1.2, the hit-and-trial balancing method.

context: Balance the following chemical equations.
stem: \(\text{BaCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4 + \text{HCl}\)
solution:
\(\text{BaCl}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4 + 2\text{HCl}\)

Barium chloride supplies two chlorine atoms, so 2 molecules of hydrogen chloride are formed.

Check: Ba 1 and 1; Cl 2 and 2; H 2 and 2; S 1 and 1; O 4 and 4.
groundedIn: §1.1.2, the hit-and-trial balancing method.

context: Write the balanced chemical equations for the following reactions.
stem: Calcium hydroxide + Carbon dioxide \(\rightarrow\) Calcium carbonate + Water
solution:
\(\text{Ca(OH)}_2(aq) + \text{CO}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{CaCO}_3(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\)

The equation is balanced as written: Ca 1 and 1; O 4 and 4; H 2 and 2; C 1 and 1. This is the reaction that turns lime water milky.
groundedIn: §1.2.1, which gives this reaction as Eq. (1.14) following the slaked-lime discussion.

context: Write the balanced chemical equations for the following reactions.
stem: Zinc + Silver nitrate \(\rightarrow\) Zinc nitrate + Silver
solution:
\(\text{Zn}(s) + 2\text{AgNO}_3(aq) \rightarrow \text{Zn(NO}_3)_2(aq) + 2\text{Ag}(s)\)

Zinc nitrate needs two nitrate groups, so 2 molecules of silver nitrate are required and 2 atoms of silver are set free.

Check: Zn 1 and 1; Ag 2 and 2; N 2 and 2; O 6 and 6.
groundedIn: §1.2.3 — zinc is more reactive than silver and displaces it from its compound.

context: Write the balanced chemical equations for the following reactions.
stem: Aluminium + Copper chloride \(\rightarrow\) Aluminium chloride + Copper
solution:
\(2\text{Al}(s) + 3\text{CuCl}_2(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{AlCl}_3(aq) + 3\text{Cu}(s)\)

Aluminium chloride carries three chlorine atoms per aluminium, so the smallest whole-number balance takes 2 aluminium and 3 copper chloride.

Check: Al 2 and 2; Cu 3 and 3; Cl 6 and 6.
groundedIn: §1.2.3 — aluminium is more reactive than copper and displaces it from its compound.

context: Write the balanced chemical equations for the following reactions.
stem: Barium chloride + Potassium sulphate \(\rightarrow\) Barium sulphate + Potassium chloride
solution:
\(\text{BaCl}_2(aq) + \text{K}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s) + 2\text{KCl}(aq)\)

The two compounds exchange ions, so this is a double displacement reaction. Barium sulphate is insoluble and comes down as a white precipitate.

Check: Ba 1 and 1; Cl 2 and 2; K 2 and 2; S 1 and 1; O 4 and 4.
groundedIn: §1.2.4 — two different ions are exchanged, as in Activity 1.10.

context: Write the balanced chemical equation for the following and identify the type of reaction in each case.
stem: Potassium bromide(aq) + Barium iodide(aq) \(\rightarrow\) Potassium iodide(aq) + Barium bromide(s)
solution:
\(2\text{KBr}(aq) + \text{BaI}_2(aq) \rightarrow 2\text{KI}(aq) + \text{BaBr}_2(s)\)

**Type: double displacement reaction.** The potassium and barium ions exchange partners — bromide moves to barium and iodide to potassium.

Check: K 2 and 2; Br 2 and 2; Ba 1 and 1; I 2 and 2.
groundedIn: §1.2.4 — 'two different atoms or groups of atoms (ions) are exchanged in double displacement reactions'.

context: Write the balanced chemical equation for the following and identify the type of reaction in each case.
stem: Zinc carbonate(s) \(\rightarrow\) Zinc oxide(s) + Carbon dioxide(g)
solution:
\(\text{ZnCO}_3(s) \rightarrow \text{ZnO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)\)

**Type: decomposition reaction.** A single substance breaks down into two simpler substances. The equation is balanced as written: Zn 1 and 1; C 1 and 1; O 3 and 3.
groundedIn: §1.2.2 — 'a single substance decomposes to give two or more substances', the pattern of Eq. (1.19) for calcium carbonate.

context: Write the balanced chemical equation for the following and identify the type of reaction in each case.
stem: Hydrogen(g) + Chlorine(g) \(\rightarrow\) Hydrogen chloride(g)
solution:
\(\text{H}_2(g) + \text{Cl}_2(g) \rightarrow 2\text{HCl}(g)\)

**Type: combination reaction.** Two substances combine to form a single new substance.

Check: H 2 and 2; Cl 2 and 2.
groundedIn: §1.2.1 — 'a reaction in which a single product is formed from two or more reactants is known as a combination reaction'.

context: Write the balanced chemical equation for the following and identify the type of reaction in each case.
stem: Magnesium(s) + Hydrochloric acid(aq) \(\rightarrow\) Magnesium chloride(aq) + Hydrogen(g)
solution:
\(\text{Mg}(s) + 2\text{HCl}(aq) \rightarrow \text{MgCl}_2(aq) + \text{H}_2(g)\)

**Type: displacement reaction.** Magnesium is more reactive than hydrogen, so it displaces hydrogen from the acid.

Check: Mg 1 and 1; H 2 and 2; Cl 2 and 2.
groundedIn: §1.2.3 — 'when an element displaces another element from its compound, a displacement reaction occurs'.

stem: What does one mean by exothermic and endothermic reactions? Give examples.
solution:
**Exothermic reactions** are reactions in which heat is given out along with the products.

Examples:

- Burning of natural gas: \(\text{CH}_4(g) + 2\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow \text{CO}_2(g) + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}(g) + \text{Heat}\)
- Slaking of quick lime: \(\text{CaO}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2(aq) + \text{Heat}\)

**Endothermic reactions** are reactions in which energy is absorbed.

Examples:

- Decomposition of calcium carbonate on heating: \(\text{CaCO}_3(s) \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} \text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)\)
- Decomposition of water by electricity: \(2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \xrightarrow{\text{Electricity}} 2\text{H}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g)\)
groundedIn: §1.2.1 defines the exothermic case and §1.2.2 the endothermic one — 'reactions in which energy is absorbed are known as endothermic reactions'.

stem: Why is respiration considered an exothermic reaction? Explain.
solution:
Respiration is the process by which the glucose obtained from our food is broken down with the oxygen we breathe in:

\(\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}\text{O}_6(aq) + 6\text{O}_2(g) \rightarrow 6\text{CO}_2(g) + 6\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) + \text{Energy}\)

Energy is **released** along with the products, and that released energy is what keeps the body warm and powers every activity in it. A reaction that gives out heat along with its products is by definition exothermic, so respiration is an exothermic reaction.
groundedIn: §1.2.1, which gives respiration as its worked example of an exothermic reaction.

stem: Why are decomposition reactions called the opposite of combination reactions? Write equations for these reactions.
solution:
In a **combination** reaction two or more substances join to give a *single* product. In a **decomposition** reaction a *single* substance splits to give two or more products. Each undoes what the other does, which is why decomposition is described as the opposite of combination.

Combination:

\(\text{CaO}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow \text{Ca(OH)}_2(aq)\)

Decomposition:

\(\text{CaCO}_3(s) \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} \text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)\)

A second difference follows from the first: combination reactions are usually exothermic, while decomposition reactions need energy — as heat, light or electricity — supplied to break the reactant down.
groundedIn: §1.2.2 — 'decomposition reactions are opposite to combination reactions'; the equations are Eq. (1.13) and Eq. (1.19).

stem: Write one equation each for decomposition reactions where energy is supplied in the form of heat, light or electricity.
solution:
**Heat** — limestone decomposes on strong heating:

\(\text{CaCO}_3(s) \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} \text{CaO}(s) + \text{CO}_2(g)\)

**Light** — silver chloride turns grey in sunlight:

\(2\text{AgCl}(s) \xrightarrow{\text{Sunlight}} 2\text{Ag}(s) + \text{Cl}_2(g)\)

**Electricity** — water is decomposed by passing a current through it:

\(2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \xrightarrow{\text{Electricity}} 2\text{H}_2(g) + \text{O}_2(g)\)
groundedIn: §1.2.2, Eq. (1.19), Eq. (1.22) and the electrolysis of Activity 1.7 — 'decomposition reactions require energy either in the form of heat, light or electricity'.

stem: What is the difference between displacement and double displacement reactions? Write equations for these reactions.
solution:
In a **displacement** reaction a single, more reactive element pushes a less reactive element out of its compound. Only one exchange happens, and one of the reactants is a free element:

\(\text{Fe}(s) + \text{CuSO}_4(aq) \rightarrow \text{FeSO}_4(aq) + \text{Cu}(s)\)

In a **double displacement** reaction two compounds exchange their ions with each other. Both reactants are compounds, usually in solution, and a precipitate often forms:

\(\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) + \text{BaCl}_2(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s) + 2\text{NaCl}(aq)\)
groundedIn: §1.2.3 and §1.2.4; the equations are Eq. (1.24) and the reaction of Activity 1.10.

stem: In the refining of silver, the recovery of silver from silver nitrate solution involved displacement by copper metal. Write down the reaction involved.
solution:
\(\text{Cu}(s) + 2\text{AgNO}_3(aq) \rightarrow \text{Cu(NO}_3)_2(aq) + 2\text{Ag}(s)\)

Copper is more reactive than silver, so it displaces silver from silver nitrate solution. The silver comes out as the free metal and the copper goes into solution as copper nitrate, turning the solution blue.

Check: Cu 1 and 1; Ag 2 and 2; N 2 and 2; O 6 and 6.
groundedIn: §1.2.3 — a more reactive metal displaces a less reactive one from its compound, as in Eq. (1.25) and Eq. (1.26).

stem: What do you mean by a precipitation reaction? Explain by giving examples.
solution:
A **precipitation reaction** is a reaction that produces an insoluble substance — a precipitate — when two solutions are mixed.

Example 1:

\(\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4(aq) + \text{BaCl}_2(aq) \rightarrow \text{BaSO}_4(s) + 2\text{NaCl}(aq)\)

The white substance that settles out is barium sulphate, which is insoluble in water.

Example 2:

\(\text{Pb(NO}_3)_2(aq) + 2\text{KI}(aq) \rightarrow \text{PbI}_2(s) + 2\text{KNO}_3(aq)\)

Here the yellow precipitate is lead iodide.
groundedIn: §1.2.4 — 'any reaction that produces a precipitate can be called a precipitation reaction'; the examples are Activity 1.10 and Activity 1.2.

context: Explain the following in terms of gain or loss of oxygen with two examples each.
stem: Oxidation
solution:
**Oxidation** is the gain of oxygen by a substance during a reaction.

Example 1 — copper gains oxygen on heating in air:

\(2\text{Cu}(s) + \text{O}_2(g) \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} 2\text{CuO}(s)\)

Example 2 — carbon gains oxygen when zinc oxide is heated with it:

\(\text{ZnO}(s) + \text{C}(s) \rightarrow \text{Zn}(s) + \text{CO}(g)\)

Here the carbon is oxidised to carbon monoxide.
groundedIn: §1.2.5 — 'if a substance gains oxygen ... it is oxidised'; the examples are Activity 1.11 and Eq. (1.31).

context: Explain the following in terms of gain or loss of oxygen with two examples each.
stem: Reduction
solution:
**Reduction** is the loss of oxygen by a substance during a reaction.

Example 1 — copper oxide loses oxygen when heated with hydrogen:

\(\text{CuO}(s) + \text{H}_2(g) \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} \text{Cu}(s) + \text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\)

Example 2 — zinc oxide loses oxygen when heated with carbon:

\(\text{ZnO}(s) + \text{C}(s) \rightarrow \text{Zn}(s) + \text{CO}(g)\)

In both reactions the metal oxide is reduced while the other reactant is oxidised, so each is a redox reaction.
groundedIn: §1.2.5 — 'if a substance loses oxygen ... it is reduced'; the examples are Eq. (1.30) and Eq. (1.31).

stem: A shiny brown coloured element 'X' on heating in air becomes black in colour. Name the element 'X' and the black coloured compound formed.
solution:
'X' is **copper**, \(\text{Cu}\) — the shiny brown metal.

On heating in air, copper combines with the oxygen of the air and its surface becomes coated with a black substance, **copper(II) oxide**, \(\text{CuO}\):

\(2\text{Cu}(s) + \text{O}_2(g) \xrightarrow{\text{Heat}} 2\text{CuO}(s)\)

The copper has gained oxygen, so it has been oxidised.
groundedIn: Activity 1.11 and §1.2.5, where copper powder heated in a china dish is coated with black copper(II) oxide.

stem: Why do we apply paint on iron articles?
solution:
Iron articles corrode when they are attacked by the moisture, oxygen and acids in the air around them, becoming coated with a reddish-brown powder — this is rusting.

Painting an iron article puts a continuous layer between the metal and the air, so moisture and oxygen cannot reach the iron surface and rusting is prevented. This matters because corrosion damages car bodies, bridges, iron railings and ships, and an enormous amount of money is spent every year replacing damaged iron.
groundedIn: §1.3.1 — 'when a metal is attacked by substances around it such as moisture, acids, etc., it is said to corrode and this process is called corrosion'.

stem: Oil and fat containing food items are flushed with nitrogen. Why?
solution:
When fats and oils are oxidised they become rancid, and their smell and taste change.

Nitrogen is an unreactive gas. Flushing the packet with nitrogen drives out the air, so the oxygen that would otherwise oxidise the fats and oils is no longer in contact with the food. Without oxygen the oxidation cannot take place, so the food does not turn rancid and keeps for longer. This is why manufacturers flush bags of chips with nitrogen.
groundedIn: §1.3.2 — 'when fats and oils are oxidised, they become rancid ... chips manufacturers usually flush bags of chips with gas such as nitrogen to prevent the chips from getting oxidised'.

context: Explain the following terms with one example each.
stem: Corrosion
solution:
**Corrosion** is the process in which a metal is slowly eaten away by the substances around it — moisture, oxygen, acids and so on — and becomes coated with a different substance.

Example: iron articles are shiny when new, but on being left in damp air they become coated with a reddish-brown powder. This is the rusting of iron:

\(4\text{Fe}(s) + 3\text{O}_2(g) + 2x\text{H}_2\text{O}(l) \rightarrow 2\text{Fe}_2\text{O}_3 \cdot x\text{H}_2\text{O}(s)\)

The black coating that forms on silver and the green coating on copper are other examples of corrosion.
groundedIn: §1.3.1 — the definition of corrosion and the rusting, tarnishing and green-coating examples.

context: Explain the following terms with one example each.
stem: Rancidity
solution:
**Rancidity** is the change in smell and taste that fat- and oil-containing foods undergo when they are oxidised on standing for a long time.

Example: a packet of fried snacks or a tin of ghee left open for some weeks develops an unpleasant smell and taste, because the fat in it has been oxidised by the oxygen of the air.

Rancidity is slowed down by adding antioxidants to the food, by keeping the food in air-tight containers, and by flushing the packet with an unreactive gas such as nitrogen.
groundedIn: §1.3.2 — 'when fats and oils are oxidised, they become rancid and their smell and taste change', with antioxidants and air-tight containers as the remedies.
